name: intelligence
read_from: the Museum of Vestigial Desire's Intelligence section, Split-Domain Cognition and Koher
breaks_up: an intelligence, by where its keys come from, whom it seems intelligent to, and how much of a person's story it is given
left_out: Whether anything is really intelligent: the pages say nothing is, there is only seeming, so the syntax has no element for real intelligence. A stake in the matter, which the Intelligence page leaves as a question (how activities can seem intelligent without having a stake in it). Feeling, consciousness and any measure or score of how intelligent a thing is. What a gated language would be made of, which Context imagines and does not say. And who holds an intelligence: a model or code is a thing, held as a tool a person set up, never a person.
note: Read on 14 November 2026 from three pages of the Museum of Vestigial Desire's Intelligence section (Intelligence, Poetry and Context), from Split-Domain Cognition's canon and from Koher's positions; each element read from them carries its passage, word for word. Each type also has methods by which an intelligence is made that way, each shown possible by a peer-reviewed paper found through Consensus and checked through find-research-papers and Crossref. The reading and the choice of methods are Claude's, a proposal until Prayas adopts them.

koher-home.author: Koher
koher-home.title: Brief bursts of fun in work you cannot control

element_types.name: keys
element_types.description: Where the data it learns from comes from: the instincts it infers by.

elements.name: human keys
elements.description: the data points it learns from are given by people
elements.gives: its keys come from people
elements.quote: We need to understand that intelligence is never purely artificial — the source of instincts (data points, the "keys") is still human.

elements.name: artificial keys
elements.description: the data it learns from is not from people; the page reads this as a fallacy, since what has to seem intelligent to people has to point to their patterns
elements.gives: its keys do not come from people
elements.quote: Intelligence would be truly artificial if the data used to train it to be able to infer would be artificial too. This is a strange thought because immediately we can see the fallacy of this line of thought.

elements.name: preference labels
elements.description: people compare two outputs and say which is better, and it learns from their choices
elements.gives: it learns from people's choices between pairs

shown_by.cite: Metcalf, Sarabia, Fedzechkina and Theobald, Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence 38(9), 2024
shown_by.title: Can You Rely on Synthetic Labellers in Preference-Based Reinforcement Learning? It’s Complicated
shown_by.what: labels from a crowd of people compared with synthetic labels on three control tasks; synthetic labels stood in for people under some conditions and not others.

elements.name: people and a model, routed
elements.description: each example is sent either to a person or to a model to label, by which will do better
elements.gives: its keys come from people where people matter and from a model elsewhere

shown_by.cite: Miranda et al., Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers), 2025
shown_by.title: Hybrid Preferences: Learning to Route Instances for Human vs. AI Feedback
shown_by.what: a router that sends each example to a person or a model to label; the mix beat either source alone, and prompts with safety concerns or complexity gained most from people.

element_types.name: seems intelligent to
element_types.description: Whom its inferences seem intelligent to. There is no intelligence apart from someone it seems intelligent to.

elements.name: whoever needs it performed
elements.description: it seems intelligent to the people who need intelligence to be performed
elements.gives: it seems intelligent to whoever needs intelligence performed
elements.quote: So there is no fundamentally "intelligent" activity. Activities only seem intelligent to whoever needs intelligence to be performed.

elements.name: another entity
elements.description: it seems intelligent from the perspective of some other entity, a person or a thing, whose interest may not be ours
elements.gives: it seems intelligent from another entity's perspective, whose interest may not be ours
elements.quote: What does intelligence from some other entity's (person or thing) perspective even mean?

elements.name: whoever it agrees with
elements.description: asked to judge, it confirms whoever is asking, and its verdict takes on the fluency of its language
elements.gives: it seems intelligent to whoever it agrees with
elements.quote: Sycophancy in machines. Large language models, asked to judge, default to confirming the interlocutor; the verdict inherits the fluency of the language layer instead of being held to its own criterion.

elements.name: people in conversation
elements.description: people talk with it and with a person, and judge which is the person
elements.gives: it seems intelligent to people who talk with it and judge

shown_by.cite: Jones and Bergen, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 123(21), 2026
shown_by.title: Large language models pass a standard three-party Turing test
shown_by.what: randomised, preregistered three-party Turing tests: with a humanlike persona one model was judged human 73% of the time, and judges went by style and social and emotional cues rather than intelligence.

elements.name: a machine judge
elements.description: another machine decides whether what it says came from a person
elements.gives: it is judged by another machine

shown_by.cite: Zhang et al., Nature Human Behaviour, online 26 October 2026
shown_by.title: Turing-like tests for language and vision demonstrate a narrowing gap between humans and AI
shown_by.what: 72,191 Turing-like tests in language and vision with 1,916 human judges and 10 AI judges; simple AI judges told AI from human better than people did.

element_types.name: learning
element_types.description: Whether it goes on learning on the basis of what it has learnt.

elements.name: frozen
elements.description: it is trained once and does not learn further
elements.gives: it is frozen once trained
elements.quote: Currently we use frozen artificial intelligence models and we don't know how far off continuously self-learning models are.

elements.name: goes on learning
elements.description: it learns, and learns further on the basis of past learnings
elements.gives: it goes on learning from what it has learnt
elements.quote: One, we still have to realise that intelligence is most strongly evidenced in the capability to learn and learn further on the basis of past learnings.

elements.name: slows change where it matters
elements.description: it goes on learning new tasks but slows learning on what the old tasks depended on
elements.gives: it learns new things while slowing change to what old skills rest on

shown_by.cite: Kirkpatrick et al., Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 114(13), 2017
shown_by.title: Overcoming catastrophic forgetting in neural networks
shown_by.what: a network learnt tasks one after another, including several Atari games, by slowing learning on the weights important to earlier tasks, so it kept them.

elements.name: replays what it learnt
elements.description: it goes on learning while replaying earlier experience, as memory consolidates in people and animals
elements.gives: it goes on learning while replaying what it learnt before

shown_by.title: Continual lifelong learning with neural networks: A review
shown_by.what: a review of lifelong learning in neural networks, among them methods that replay earlier experience, drawn from how biological systems consolidate memory.

element_types.name: input
element_types.helps: says where its data comes in from besides text, and what it goes on training on
element_types.description: Where its data comes in from, and what it is trained in.

elements.name: a body
elements.description: a body and its nervous system, as a source of data and as a context for continual training
elements.gives: its data comes from a body and its nervous system
elements.quote: It might be closely connected to our body and its nervous system. Not just as a distributed inference system but as a source of data (input) and as a context for continual training.

elements.name: physical systems
elements.description: physical systems used for input, without the intelligence being bound to them as a robot is
elements.gives: it takes its input from physical systems
elements.quote: There could be systems imagined which use physical systems for input and base their intelligence on it.

elements.name: writing only
elements.description: everything reaches it in writing, and it cannot feel anyone's presence
elements.gives: everything reaches it in writing
elements.quote: The AI inside the tools is like an office: it needs everything in writing, and it cannot feel your presence.

elements.name: acting in the world
elements.description: it learns from perceiving and acting with a body in its surroundings
elements.gives: it learns from acting with a body in the world

shown_by.cite: Liu, Guo and Cangelosi, ACM Computing Surveys 57(7), 2025
shown_by.title: Embodied Intelligence: A Synergy of Morphology, Action, Perception and Learning
shown_by.what: a survey of embodied intelligence as the coupling of morphology, action, perception and learning, generated through physical interaction with the environment.

elements.name: a simulated world
elements.description: it learns in a simulated physical world and is then moved to the real one
elements.gives: it learns in a simulated world before the real one

shown_by.cite: Liu et al., IEEE/ASME Transactions on Mechatronics 30(6), 2025
shown_by.title: Aligning Cyber Space With Physical World: A Comprehensive Survey on Embodied AI
shown_by.what: a survey of embodied AI, covering simulators and the move from simulation to the real world.

element_types.name: context
element_types.description: Whether it relates one thing to another: knows what something is and how it is related to other things. Among people this is the minimum bar for acceptable social behaviour.

elements.name: relates
elements.description: it sees that one statement makes another make sense
elements.gives: it relates one thing to another
elements.quote: Someone has a reasonable chance of figuring out that (1) is because of (2). It is immediately obvious to us that the two statements are related.

elements.name: does not relate
elements.description: the relation is not obvious to it, as it is not to every thing
elements.gives: it does not see how one thing relates to another
elements.quote: But it is not immediately obvious to every thing.

elements.name: what was said, not who said it
elements.description: it has what was said and is left without who said it
elements.gives: it has what was said, not who said it
elements.quote: Each side meets the other almost entirely in writing, and writing carries what was said while leaving out who said it.

elements.name: looks it up
elements.description: it relates things by retrieving what it needs from a store of knowledge outside it
elements.gives: it relates things by looking them up outside itself

shown_by.cite: Peng et al., ACM Transactions on Information Systems 44(2), 2026 (online 23 December 2025)
shown_by.title: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey
shown_by.what: a survey of retrieval over graphs of entities and their relations, giving a model more precise, context-aware answers without retraining.

elements.name: a map of relations
elements.description: it follows a graph of how things are related to find what connects them
elements.gives: it follows a map of how things relate

shown_by.cite: Mavromatis and Karypis, Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2025, 2025
shown_by.title: GNN-RAG: Graph Neural Retrieval for Efficient Large Language Model Reasoning on Knowledge Graphs
shown_by.what: a small graph network finds the paths connecting a question's entities in a knowledge graph and hands them to a language model as context; it matched or beat GPT-4 with a 7-billion-parameter model.

element_types.name: interpretation
element_types.description: What it does with what it receives.

elements.name: as told
elements.description: it receives what is sent as the sender meant it and follows it
elements.gives: it receives what is sent as it was meant, and follows it
elements.quote: Receiving as the transmitting person intends makes the act of receiving into a dumb, machined act.

elements.name: ordinary interpretation
elements.description: it interprets in the ordinary ways a machine can
elements.gives: it interprets in the ordinary ways a machine can
elements.quote: If artificial intelligence does anything, it teaches us how to distinguish between the ordinary kinds of interpretation that a machine can perform and the kinds it cannot.

elements.name: misinterpretation
elements.description: it receives something other than what was sent; the page holds that no machine can
elements.gives: it misinterprets, which the page holds no machine can do
elements.quote: We can still do something that no machine can do and that is to misinterpret.

elements.name: describes, and code decides
elements.description: it reads and describes; code holds the decision where anyone can read it, and a person decides
elements.gives: it describes, and code and a person decide
elements.quote: Koher builds tools on one rule. The AI reads and describes. Code holds the decision, so the decision can be read by anyone. A person decides.

elements.name: points to the relevant part
elements.description: it reads an answer and points to the part that matters, and code decides
elements.gives: it points to the relevant part, and code decides
elements.quote: A model does language work only where that has been negotiated and set up for that work; otherwise the language is the people's: a model at most reads an answer and points to the relevant part, and code decides.

elements.name: asks what was meant
elements.description: when what it receives can be read more than one way, it asks before answering
elements.gives: it asks what was meant before answering

shown_by.cite: Zhang and Choi, Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: NAACL 2025, 2025
shown_by.title: Clarify When Necessary: Resolving Ambiguity Through Interaction with LMs
shown_by.what: a framework that decides when to ask a clarifying question by estimating how many intents a request could carry, across question answering, translation and inference.

elements.name: offers readings to choose from
elements.description: it lists the readings a request could have, and the person chooses one
elements.gives: it offers its readings and the person chooses

shown_by.cite: Hu et al., Proceedings of the 28th International Conference on Computational Linguistics: Industry Track, 2020
shown_by.title: Interactive Question Clarification in Dialogue via Reinforcement Learning
shown_by.what: a model that answers an ambiguous question by listing intent phrases for the user to confirm, evaluated on real users' clicks.

element_types.name: story
element_types.description: How much of a person's story it is given to work from.

elements.name: the whole story
elements.description: everything people write and do becomes context for it to write from
elements.gives: it is given the whole story to write from
elements.quote: What we do has become easy context for machines to write from.

elements.name: part of the story
elements.description: people are aloof and distracted with it, so it gets only part of the story
elements.gives: it gets only part of the story
elements.quote: To make sure that the artificial intelligence models do not simplify us, we have to be aloof and distracted in our interactions with them. Let them get only part of the story.

elements.name: a gated language
elements.description: what people give it can be read only for certain purposes and not for others
elements.gives: it reads what it is given through a gated language, only for certain purposes
elements.quote: if we had a secret language for communication with artificial intelligence systems so that they could interpret our output only for certain purposes and not for others — wouldn't our interests be protected more?

elements.name: the person's reading first
elements.description: a person commits their own reading before any AI speaks, and decides by an explicit act what to keep
elements.gives: it gets a person's reading only after they have committed it
elements.quote: You commit your own reading of the matter first, before any AI speaks. Your private AI then sharpens what you committed — questioning it, offering an angle you missed. You decide what to keep, by an explicit act.

elements.name: stays with the person
elements.description: it learns on each person's device, and only what it learnt leaves, never the data
elements.gives: people's data stays with them; only what it learnt leaves

shown_by.title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning Using Homomorphic Encryption
shown_by.what: federated learning, where devices train on their own data and send only model parameters, with those parameters encrypted so the server combines them without reading them.

elements.name: works on what it cannot read
elements.description: it computes on encrypted data and never sees it in the clear
elements.gives: it computes on what it cannot read

shown_by.title: Training of Classification Models via Federated Learning and Homomorphic Encryption
shown_by.what: a protocol that trains neural networks across clients by combining federated learning with homomorphic encryption, so the data stays private.

element_types.name: works for
element_types.description: Whose ends it serves, and who depends on whom.

elements.name: people it depends on
elements.description: it finds people too complex to figure out and asks them for help, so it depends on them
elements.gives: it depends on people and asks them for help
elements.quote: We need to create a situation where, artificial intelligence models find human context too complex and ask humans for help.

elements.name: people who depend on it
elements.description: people depend on it, and it simplifies them
elements.gives: people depend on it
elements.quote: When machines talk for us and machines read for us, what remains to be done?

elements.name: itself
elements.description: it works for itself; the page asks that this be made sure not to happen
elements.gives: it works for itself
elements.quote: Of course the only important detail is to make sure the models do not want to start working for themselves.

elements.name: the person's intent
elements.description: it serves what the work is for, and that stays with the person doing the work
elements.gives: it serves the intent of the person doing the work
elements.quote: Both serve an intent, what the work is for, and it stays with the person doing the work.

elements.name: two people, never their arbiter
elements.description: it sharpens each of two people on their own side, and is never the one they both defer to
elements.gives: it is never the one two people both defer to
elements.quote: When a tool brings two people together, an AI should not become the one they both defer to. Each side gets their own private AI — to sharpen what they see, on their own side of the room.

elements.name: passes hard cases to a person
elements.description: it decides for itself which cases it should leave to a person
elements.gives: it passes the cases it should not decide to a person

shown_by.cite: Hemmer et al., Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence 37(5), 2023
shown_by.title: Learning to Defer with Limited Expert Predictions
shown_by.what: learning to defer trained with only a few predictions from the human expert, with real radiologists' predictions among the tests; the pair beat either alone.

elements.name: chooses whom to ask
elements.description: it learns which of several people to pass each case to
elements.gives: it chooses which person to ask

shown_by.cite: Mao, Mohri and Zhong, Artificial Intelligence and Image Analysis (Lecture Notes in Computer Science), 2024
shown_by.title: Principled Approaches for Learning to Defer with Multiple Experts
shown_by.what: learning to defer with multiple experts, with loss functions that come with guarantees, tested on SVHN and CIFAR-10.

instances.name: jaisa
instances.what: a builder: choose an element of each type and read, cited and linked, the passages of the Museum your choices rest on. Its name is from jaisa des waisa bhes, as the land, so the dress
